session of Congress, and the publication of

NAPOLEON loved Josephine. The conqueror of Italy had laid at her feet, and whispered in her ear his tons of love as well as of ambition; her were his troubles and joys. She was ever his good genius, pointing him the path to glory and renown, and with her, his companion and adviser, he found himself upon the throne of Charlemagne. But no sooner did the diadem glitter upon his brow, than she, who had been ever true to him, was cast off for the furtherance of schemes of policy. He was thus, but he would be safer ever thus, and be procured from a weak Senate divorce from her, and wed Louise of Austria, who ascended the throne only to see his crown sink upon his brow! SIR, there may be a valuable lesson to read to our own government from the rock of St. Helena.

Rise from the mire of mere party, sustain the Administration in everything which is just and right, but resist it when its measures are hostile to the best and most enduring interests of the people. Do not enter in that unholy alliance of the purse with the sword in the hand of power: and
